label: Afternoon edition
summary: Keanu, **Wall Street had its worst day since June**: the Nasdaq fell 2.86% to 25,437, the S&P 500 lost 1.82%, and Bloomberg puts the Nasdaq about 10% below its peak (CNBC, Bloomberg). Intel dropped about 29% on weak guidance, its worst day since the 1970s, while Amazon pared a deeper early loss to close down 1.4% (CNBC, Bloomberg). Binance says hackers took **$6.3 billion, the largest crypto theft on record**, and TRM Labs and Elliptic point to North Korea (TechCrunch, Axios). Four days before the midterms, Trump reversed himself and will hold in-person rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, while CNN polls show Democrats ahead in Michigan and Texas (The Hill, CNN). A report that Democratic operatives backed a second Dan Sullivan has **roiled the Alaska Senate race**, and Peltola's campaign denies it (NPR, Fox News, The Hill). On Iran, Treasury says the blockade has **crippled Iran's economy**, and Trump says Tehran wants to talk (Axios, Fox News). In California, Prop 40 trails 46% to 52% in PPIC's poll, and no outcome was reported from the state worker mediation (CalMatters, KQED). On AI, analysts are asking what **Anthropic's IPO filing leaves out**, including about $417 billion in compute commitments (CNBC). NASA's Swift telescope is **headed for re-entry** after a failed rescue (Nature, NASA).

alerts.text: The Nasdaq fell 2.86% Friday and sits about 10% below its peak, and Apple reports Monday, Nov. 2 after the close.
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3, and Trump now plans in-person rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday.
Prop 40 trails in two polls, and Props 41 and 42 would cancel it if they get more votes.
NASA's Swift telescope could re-enter the atmosphere as soon as Nov. 2, according to some researchers.

Trump reverses his rally cancellations while CNN polls show Democrats ahead in several Senate states.
Treasury says Iran has loaded no oil since Aug. 25, and Trump says Tehran wants to talk.
Analysts question Anthropic's S-1: slower growth, $417 billion in compute commitments and no price.

watch.name: NVIDIA Corporation

stories.title: Trump reverses his rally cancellations as Democrats lead several Senate polls four days before the midterms
stories.summary: Trump will hold in-person rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday after canceling them, while CNN polls show Democrats ahead in Michigan, Texas and Kansas.
story: On Friday, Oct. 30, Trump said he will hold in-person rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, one day after the RNC and a White House official said the events were canceled in favor of tele-rallies (The Hill, CNN, NPR). Trump said friends in both states asked him to reconsider and that he would visit Iowa first, then Kansas, with another round of telephone rallies on Monday (The Hill). Officials had described the change as a scheduling rearrangement. CNN reported that Trump grew irked over coverage of the cancellations before ordering the events back on.

The states are competitive. A CNN poll has Democrat Adam Hamilton ahead of Sen. Roger Marshall 49% to 45% in Kansas, and the Cook Political Report rates both Kansas and Iowa as toss-ups. An Emerson College/The Hill poll has Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson leading Democrat Josh Turek by 2 points (The Hill). CNN's other new polls show Democrat Abdul El-Sayed ahead of Mike Rogers 49% to 42% in Michigan and Democrat James Talarico ahead of Ken Paxton 49% to 43% in Texas (CNN).

Republicans say the polls understate them. Senate Majority Leader John Thune predicts the party will outperform the polls and keep its majority, though he concedes that Mississippi and South Carolina have shifted toward Democrats. NRSC chair Tim Scott says "The momentum, frankly, is with us, not against us" (Fox News). Fox News power rankings call Senate control a toss-up. The Washington Examiner reports that RealClearPolitics averages show Democrats leading in six of eight toss-up Senate races.

A CNN analysis says the range of outcomes for the Senate is enormous. Democrats could win one of the biggest popular-vote margins in decades and still fall short of a majority, because they need a net gain of four seats from a 53-47 deficit.
facts: Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.
Trump plans Iowa and Kansas rallies on Sunday, Nov. 1, and tele-rallies on Monday.
CNN has Michigan at El-Sayed 49%, Rogers 42%, and Texas at Talarico 49%, Paxton 43%.
Democrats need a net gain of four Senate seats; Republicans hold it 53-47.
Fox News power rankings rate Senate control a toss-up.
stories.next: Polls close Tuesday, Nov. 3. Watch Iowa and Kansas returns and whether Sunday's rallies move undecided voters.
stories.flag: Officials say the rally change was about scheduling, while CNN reported Trump was reacting to coverage. Many poll leads sit inside the margin of error.
stories.left: Democrats say the president is campaigning from a defensive crouch, with rally reversals as evidence that red states are in play. They tie voter frustration to prices, the Iran war and what they see as federal pressure on election officials. Their worry is turnout and the Republican spending advantage, not the message. They note that polls in Kansas, Iowa and Texas would have looked unthinkable a year ago.
stories.right: Republicans say the map and money favor them and that polls have missed before. They argue that Thune and Scott are reading the same private data and see a majority that holds, and that the rally shuffle reflects a candidate-first strategy of telephone events to reach more states. Conservatives also say voters weighing a Democratic Senate will think about the war, the border and taxes, which polls capture poorly.

stories.title: Alaska Senate race is roiled by a report that Democratic operatives backed a second Dan Sullivan
stories.summary: A New York Times report alleges Peltola campaign and DSCC staff helped field a second candidate named Dan Sullivan, which both deny.
story: The New York Times reported that Democratic operatives tied to Mary Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee recruited a second candidate named Dan Sullivan to split votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, according to NPR, which says it has not independently confirmed the reporting. The effort was allegedly called the "ballot composition project" and began in summer 2025, when a Peltola staffer was reportedly told to comb voter rolls for Alaskans with that name (NPR, Fox News).

Peltola's campaign denies involvement and called the story "just another distraction." The DSCC says it had no involvement, and Sen. Chris Murphy blamed a "disgruntled fired former campaign staffer" (The Hill). Trump called the allegations "Voter Fraud at the Highest Level." Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation, House Oversight Chair James Comer summoned two operatives named in the report, and Sen. Lisa Murkowski also criticized the effort (The Hill, NPR).

The legal picture is murky. The Hill reports that ballot stacking is not illegal under state law, and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in June that the second Sullivan could appear on the ballot. Fox News reports the U.S. Attorney's Office in Alaska has been investigating for months and that the Justice Department sought to delay certification. Polls taken before and after the story showed Peltola ahead, and early voting was already underway, so experts quoted by The Hill doubt the story will move many voters.
National Review and the Washington Examiner opinion writers call the alleged scheme proof that Democrats think voters are easy to fool.
facts: The allegation comes from a New York Times report that NPR has not independently confirmed.
Peltola's campaign and the DSCC deny involvement.
Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation.
The second Sullivan changed his registration from Republican to undeclared, per the Alaska Beacon as reported by NPR.
Early voting was already underway when the story broke.
stories.next: Watch Alaska results on Tuesday, Nov. 3, and any Justice Department move on certification if Sullivan loses.
stories.flag: The core allegation rests on one New York Times investigation. Peltola's campaign and the DSCC deny it, and NPR has not confirmed it.
stories.left: Democrats say the story leans on a fired ex-staffer and unproven claims, and that stacking the ballot with similar names is not illegal under Alaska law. They accuse Trump and the Justice Department of using it as a pretext to question certification and chill a close race. Polls before and after the report showed Peltola ahead, and they argue voters should judge the candidates on policy.
stories.right: Republicans say that if the report is true, a campaign tried to trick voters by putting a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot to peel off votes from the incumbent. They point to Murkowski's criticism as proof the concern crosses party lines, and argue that Democrats who preach about election integrity must answer questions. Sullivan's camp calls it a deliberate deception, and they want investigators to finish their work before certification.

stories.title: Treasury says the Iran blockade has crippled its economy as Trump says Tehran wants to talk
stories.summary: A Treasury assessment says Iran has loaded no oil since Aug. 25, while Trump predicts the war ends 'very soon' and strike options stay ready.
story: A Treasury Department assessment says the U.S. naval blockade, sanctions and pressure on overland export routes have crippled Iran's economy and cut its revenue, Axios reported on Friday, Oct. 30. The report says Iran has not loaded any oil onto tankers since Aug. 25, that the rial has fallen about a quarter since August and that annual inflation hit 90% in September. It does not argue the regime is near collapse (Axios). Thousands of trucks are stranded at the Turkish border, with delays of up to 20 days.

Trump said Friday that Iran wants to talk and predicted the war would end "very soon," while saying Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon (Fox News). Tehran has not answered the letter Vice President Vance sent to security chief Mohsen Rezaei this week and says the U.S. must lift the blockade before talks begin. It also wants frozen funds released and oil sales allowed (Axios, Fox News).

The military track continues. Adm. Brad Cooper, the top U.S. Middle East commander, briefed Trump on Thursday on whether the blockade is working, and officials say strike options are being readied for after the Nov. 3 midterms (Axios, Fox News). Earlier Fox News coverage found an estimated 80 million barrels of Iranian crude in floating storage, citing Reuters, and a former Treasury official said the blockade is not stopping oil already past the line.
Oil still matters to households. WTI crude settled near $103 on Friday (market data).
facts: Treasury says Iran has loaded no oil onto tankers since Aug. 25.
The rial has fallen about 25% since August and inflation reached 90% in September, per the Treasury report.
Iran has not replied to Vance's letter and demands the blockade end first.
Adm. Brad Cooper briefed Trump on the blockade on Thursday, Oct. 29.
WTI crude was $102.95 on Friday.
stories.next: Watch for an Iranian reply to Vance and any strike order after Tuesday's election.
stories.flag: The Treasury report is described through Axios and administration officials, and independent verification of its figures was not found. Fox News has reported oil still moving past the blockade line.
stories.blindspot: Coverage found came mostly from Axios and Fox News; no left-leaning outlet's take on the Treasury report was found.
stories.left: Critics say the blockade imposes heavy costs on Iranian civilians and on American households through oil near $103, and that the administration is threatening a larger strike while also writing letters. They argue a deal that trades verified nuclear limits for sanctions relief is the realistic exit. Many Democrats also say a bigger campaign needs congressional approval.
stories.right: Conservatives say the Treasury figures show the pressure strategy working and that Iran only talks when it is squeezed. They argue that sanctions relief before nuclear concessions rewards stalling, and that strike options are the credible threat behind diplomacy. Some on the right warn that the Fox News reporting on floating oil shows leaks must be closed before the pressure is complete.

stories.title: Judge rejects DOJ bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots, and subpoenas to election workers follow
stories.summary: Judge David Carter refused to make California segregate ballots tied to suspected noncitizens. The DOJ appealed, and grand jury subpoenas reached election staff.
story: U.S. District Judge David Carter denied the Justice Department's emergency request on Wednesday, Oct. 28, to make California set aside mail ballots linked to about 20,000 voters that federal officials call likely noncitizens. He wrote that the request would "wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway" (CNN, NPR). He also said the government's methodology raised reliability questions and that federal prosecutors can still pursue individual cases (CNN, NPR, Fox News). The DOJ appealed to the Ninth Circuit right away (CalMatters).

California officials say some names on the list are not on their rolls or are in suspended status, and a preliminary review found U.S.-born people on it (Fox News, CalMatters). A top federal prosecutor in California says investigators determined all 20,000 flagged people are not citizens (Fox News). That claim has not been independently verified in the coverage found. The Ninth Circuit had earlier dismissed an emergency DOJ request, 2-1, because Carter had not yet ruled (Washington Examiner).

On Thursday, at least four California election workers received federal grand jury subpoenas, at least one after Carter ordered the DOJ to stop threatening officials (CalMatters, NPR). Orange County's subpoena seeks unredacted records for about 60 people. Three Los Angeles employees were told to appear in Santa Ana on Nov. 4. DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels said receiving a subpoena does not make someone a target. Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan called the approach "confrontational, adversarial" (CalMatters).
The fight could still reach the Supreme Court, and it lands in the same week California counts ballots for Tuesday's election.
stories.flag: The DOJ's claim that all 20,000 people are noncitizens is disputed by state officials and not independently verified.
facts: Carter ruled on Wednesday, Oct. 28, and denied the request to segregate about 20,000 ballots.
The DOJ appealed to the Ninth Circuit after the ruling.
At least four California election workers got federal grand jury subpoenas in the past week.
Three Los Angeles employees must appear in Santa Ana on Nov. 4.
Orange County's subpoena seeks unredacted voter records for about 60 people.
stories.left: Democrats and election officials say the DOJ is trying to disrupt a vote already underway on thin evidence. They point to Carter's finding that the list is unreliable, to U.S.-born people found on it, and to subpoenas served after a judge told prosecutors to stop threatening officials. They argue that states run elections, and that individual fraud cases are the proper route.
stories.right: Conservatives argue that counting ballots from people who are not citizens cannot be undone once those ballots are mixed in, so setting them aside costs little. They say California refused to cooperate with a legitimate federal request, as election-law expert Hans von Spakovsky has argued, and that DOJ prosecutors verified the names. In this view, a state that will not fix its rolls invites federal action.
stories.next: The Ninth Circuit is expected to rule on the new appeal, and Los Angeles election staff face the Nov. 4 grand jury date.

stories.title: California and its largest state worker union meet in mediation after the first strike in 44 years
stories.summary: SEIU Local 1000 and the Newsom administration met with a state mediator on Friday, but no outcome had been reported.
story: SEIU Local 1000, California's largest state employee union, and the Newsom administration were scheduled to resume mediation on Friday, Oct. 30, nine days after thousands of members walked off the job for one day. It was the union's first strike in 44 years (CalMatters, KQED). The state Public Employment Relations Board appointed the mediator. The union wants higher pay, larger state contributions to health coverage and changes to the order that most state employees work in the office four days a week.

That order took effect in July after a one-year delay (CalMatters). Newsom vetoed AB 1729, a bill to loosen telework rules, last month. In late September the labor board found that the state's human resources department "refused to meet and confer in good faith" (CalMatters).

The state says it remains at the table and points to the union's refusal to move on return to office. The union says the administration rejected proposals without bargaining over them and has filed a complaint with the labor board (KQED, CalMatters).
Newsom leaves office in January, so the union is trying to settle before the next governor arrives.
stories.blindspot: Covered mainly by California public-affairs and left-leaning outlets; no right-leaning coverage found.
facts: The one-day strike was Oct. 21, SEIU Local 1000's first in 44 years.
Mediation was scheduled for Friday, Oct. 30.
Newsom's order requires most state employees in the office four days a week.
Newsom vetoed telework bill AB 1729 last month.
The labor board found in September that the state refused to bargain in good faith.
stories.left: Labor advocates say workers have gone years without a raise that matches rent and health costs, and that a four-day office order costs them commuting time and money. They argue the labor board's finding shows the state bargained in bad faith. For them, a strike was a last resort.
stories.right: Critics say a union striking while California faces budget pressure puts workers ahead of taxpayers. They support returning state workers to offices to serve the public and keep downtown Sacramento running. They also say pay and benefits should be weighed against a state deficit that Sacramento keeps papering over.
stories.next: Watch for word on a tentative agreement or a second strike notice, since Newsom leaves office in January.
stories.flag: Coverage found does not report whether Friday's mediation produced progress or a tentative deal.

stories.title: Prop 40 billionaire tax trails in two polls as opponents outspend backers more than six to one
stories.summary: PPIC has 46% for and 52% against, Berkeley IGS has 42% for and 50% against, and Props 41 and 42 would cancel the tax if they win more votes.
story: California's proposed billionaire tax, Prop 40, is losing ground with days to go. The latest PPIC survey of 1,086 likely voters has 46% in favor and 52% opposed, a drop from last month, when supporters had a slim majority. The Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies finds 42% yes and 50% no (CalMatters, KQED). A Citrin-Politico poll had support at 46% and opposition at 43%. Props 41 and 42 were put on the ballot by billionaire-backed groups to cancel the tax.

If Prop 40 gets more votes than both, the tax takes effect. If either passes with more votes, it does not (CalMatters). Opponents have raised more than $205 million, including at least $102 million from Google co-founder Sergey Brin, while backers raised about $31 million, mostly from unions (CalMatters).

Gov. Gavin Newsom opposes the measure and backs a federal billionaire tax instead. So do the three leading governor candidates (CalMatters). Fox Business has covered Brin's move of entities out of California and his comparison of the tax to Soviet socialism. Critics also object that the tax reaches people who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026, even if they left.
California votes Tuesday, Nov. 3. CalMatters notes the measure might not become law even if it passes.
stories.flag: Spending totals differ by outlet: Fox Business cited smaller Brin figures from earlier in the year than CalMatters' $102 million.
facts: PPIC has Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no among likely voters.
Berkeley IGS has 42% yes and 50% no.
Opponents have raised over $205 million; backers about $31 million.
Props 41 and 42 would cancel the tax if they get more votes than Prop 40.
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.
stories.left: Supporters say a small group of billionaires is spending nine figures to avoid a tax that would fund health care, and that the spending gap shows why the tax is needed. They note Newsom and most of the Democratic establishment sided with the wealthy donors. The Democratic Party's own endorsement of the measure, they say, reflects voters' anger about inequality.
stories.right: Opponents argue the tax drives founders and capital out of state, which shrinks the revenue base Sacramento depends on. They call the retroactive reach unfair and say illiquid startup founders could owe huge sums on paper wealth. Garry Tan of Y Combinator said it would hurt startups. Even Newsom says it would be damaging.
stories.next: Voters decide Prop 40, 41 and 42 on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

stories.title: Local ceasefire in southern Ukraine runs through Saturday as Russian strikes hit cities and Zelenskyy floats a frozen front
stories.summary: A Melania Trump-brokered pause lets aid reach occupied Oleshky, while strikes continue elsewhere and Zelenskyy says he would freeze the front lines.
story: A local ceasefire brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump took effect early Tuesday, Oct. 27, ahead of a humanitarian mission to the occupied southern Ukrainian town of Oleshky, where up to 2,000 people are stranded. It is due to last through Saturday or longer, as missile attacks resumed in Kyiv (NPR). Deep mistrust has thwarted earlier ceasefire attempts, NPR notes.

Fighting continues elsewhere. CNBC reported on Friday that Russian strikes plunged a Ukrainian city into blackout as Zelenskyy warned of more missile attacks. CNN reported that Russia struck the Dnipro train station in central Ukraine and killed 15. On Oct. 8, a Russian strike killed at least 33 people when two buses caught fire in eastern Ukraine (CNN).

Diplomacy is moving. Zelenskyy has said he is open to freezing the front lines to end the war (Fox News). A new round of U.S.-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine is expected next month (NPR). Trump said Zelenskyy "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," a claim Zelenskyy rejected (CNN). Zelenskyy says Ukraine's Starlink access for battlefield drones is still curtailed, which the Trump administration denies ordering (NPR).
facts: The Oleshky ceasefire began Tuesday, Oct. 27, and is due to last through Saturday, Oct. 31.
Up to 2,000 people are stranded in Oleshky.
Zelenskyy says he is open to freezing the front lines.
A new round of U.S.-brokered talks is expected next month.
Russian missile attacks continued in Kyiv and other cities.
stories.next: Watch whether the Oleshky pause is extended past Saturday and when the next round of talks is set.
stories.flag: The date of the Dnipro station strike was not verified in the coverage found.
stories.left: Supporters of Ukraine say a localized pause is welcome but that Moscow is exploiting talk of freezing the front line while it hits power grids and cities. They argue the U.S. should keep intelligence and Starlink access steady and press Russia, not Kyiv, to stop. A frozen line, they say, would reward aggression.
stories.right: Conservatives who back the president's approach say the war has cost tens of thousands of lives, that Trump's own casualty figure of 25,000 in a month shows the urgency, and that a freeze may be the only workable path. They argue Europe should carry more of the burden and that U.S. leverage over Kyiv is how a deal gets made.

stories.title: Third-quarter GDP beats forecasts at 3.4% while PCE inflation hits 3.6% and the Fed holds
stories.summary: The economy grew faster than expected, inflation edged up, and traders see about an 85% chance of a December rate hike.
story: The U.S. economy grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, above the 3.1% to 3.2% economists expected, after 2.2% in the second quarter. Business investment rose almost 13% on AI equipment and consumer spending rose 3.8%, while trade subtracted 3.3 percentage points (Axios, CNBC). September PCE inflation, the Fed's favored gauge, reached 3.6% over the year, up from 3.4%. Core PCE rose from 3.0% to 3.1% (CNBC, Fox Business).

On Wednesday, Oct. 28, the Fed held its rate at 3.75% to 4% on a 10-2 vote. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point hike, and it was Cook's first dissent since joining in 2022 (Axios, CNBC). It followed September's hike, the first since 2023. Chair Kevin Warsh said he does not believe in forward guidance without a crisis. Traders put the odds of a December hike at about 85% (Axios) or 82.6% (Fox Business), and Nomura's Rob Subbaraman said a 50-basis-point move could come into play (CNBC).

NPR notes the report landed days before the midterms, with a gap between the growth data and voters' frustration over living costs. Fox Business reported that Democrats call Trump a failure on inflation while the White House cites growth.
On Friday the 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.93% and WTI crude rose to $102.95 (market data). The next Fed meeting is Dec. 8-9.
facts: Q3 GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate.
September PCE inflation was 3.6% over the year.
The Fed held at 3.75% to 4% on a 10-2 vote on Oct. 28.
Cook and Hammack dissented in favor of a hike.
The next Fed meeting is Dec. 8-9.
stories.left: Democrats and many economists say the headline growth leans on AI investment while households feel inflation, tariffs and war-driven energy prices. They argue 3.6% inflation and an 80%-plus chance of another hike mean borrowing costs rise just as families struggle. They also defend the Fed's independence, noting the administration has restarted its effort to remove Cook.
stories.right: Conservatives point to strong output, 3.8% consumer spending and a record AI buildout as proof the economy works. They say inflation tied to energy and the Iran war is temporary and blame Biden-era spending for the base. Some on the right back the Fed's willingness to hike, while Trump allies want lower rates.
stories.next: Watch the October jobs and CPI reports in November and the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting.

stories.title: Nasdaq falls 2.86% as Intel plunges 29% and Amazon pares an early loss
stories.summary: Intel had its worst day since the 1970s, and the Nasdaq sits about 10% below its peak after a week of AI-spending shocks.
story: The Nasdaq fell 2.86% to 25,437.00 on Friday, Oct. 30, its worst day since June. The S&P 500 lost 1.82% to 7,580.07 and the Dow fell 1.09% to 51,770.31 (CNBC, market data). Bloomberg put the Nasdaq about 10% below its peak, close to a technical correction. Intel dropped about 29%, its worst day since the 1970s, after it guided fourth-quarter earnings to 25 cents on $15 billion to $16 billion of revenue against estimates near 43 cents and $17 billion (CNBC). The slide cut about $12 billion from the U.S. government's roughly 10% stake in Intel.

Amazon missed on third-quarter revenue and earnings and held its 2026 capex forecast near $220 billion. Bloomberg reported an intraday drop of 7.3%, but the shares pared much of that and closed down 1.41% at $240.35 (CNBC, market data). Alphabet fell 12.64% on Thursday in its worst day on record, so the two days together hit the group that has led the AI trade.

Intel's CFO David Zinsner said the PC slowdown should continue at least through the first half of next year, and CNBC tied the weak outlook to soaring memory and component costs. Bank of America and UBS downgraded the stock or cut targets. Intel's third-quarter revenue rose 21% and its data center segment grew strongly, but the guidance overshadowed both (CNBC).

Strategists are split. Bloomberg quoted one saying the market is leaving the "hopes and dreams phase" of AI and entering a "show me" phase. UBS's chief investment officer said the answer on AI demand and monetization is still yes, and BlackRock has kept its U.S. equity and AI overweights (CNBC).
facts: The Nasdaq fell 2.86% to 25,437.00, its worst day since June.
The S&P 500 fell 1.82% to 7,580.07 and the Dow 1.09% to 51,770.31.
Intel fell about 29% on weak fourth-quarter guidance.
Amazon closed down 1.41% after an intraday drop of about 7%.
Nvidia fell 4.22% to $204.64.
stories.next: Apple reports Monday, Nov. 2 after the close, and Nvidia reports Nov. 17 after the close.
stories.flag: Intel's drop was reported as 21% to 25% in early coverage and 29% in closing coverage. Amazon's intraday and closing moves differ.
stories.why: Investors have moved from asking whether AI demand exists to asking who earns a return on the build. Companies with negative free cash flow now get punished even when revenue grows. A weak PC market adds a separate hit for chipmakers.

stories.title: Applied Materials opens its roughly $5 billion EPIC chip research center in Sunnyvale
stories.summary: The center lets TSMC, Samsung, Micron and Broadcom work alongside equipment makers to cut years from the path from lab to chip.
story: Applied Materials unveiled its Equipment and Process Innovation and Commercialization center, called EPIC, in Sunnyvale, California, on Oct. 12, IEEE Spectrum reports. The company announced the project in 2023 at about $4 billion and now says it will invest roughly $5 billion. CEO Gary Dickerson describes it as a way to speed development of next-generation chips, and the stated goal is to cut by several years the time from early-stage discovery to commercialization.

TSMC, Samsung, Micron, Broadcom and others have agreed to set up inside the lab, IEEE Spectrum reports. Competing customers get their own space behind digital firewalls and physical barriers. The project did not receive federal money: Bloomberg reported in 2024 that the Commerce Department decided it did not qualify for CHIPS Act funding.

It is one of several AI-driven bets in chip research. IEEE Spectrum also reports that Micron disclosed a $10 billion, 10-year investment in its Boise, Idaho, memory research lab, and CNBC reported in September that Samsung and Micron are sounding alarms about a deep U.S. chipmaker labor shortage.
facts: EPIC opened in Sunnyvale on Oct. 12, 2026.
The investment grew from about $4 billion to about $5 billion.
TSMC, Samsung, Micron and Broadcom are among the customers.
Competing customers are separated by digital firewalls and physical barriers.
Micron separately plans $10 billion over 10 years in Boise.
stories.next: Watch for the first process results out of EPIC and whether the labor shortage slows the new labs.
stories.flag: IEEE Spectrum sources differ slightly on timing: one older piece says the center would open in 2026, another dates the opening to Oct. 12.
stories.why: Chips now take years to move from lab to fab, and AI demand is pulling capital into shortening that gap. A shared center in Silicon Valley also gives competitors a way to test processes without building their own lines.

stories.title: Binance says hackers took $6.3 billion, the largest crypto theft on record, after a compromised engineer laptop
stories.summary: Binance traced the breach to an engineer's laptop, and TRM Labs and Elliptic attribute it to North Korean hackers.
story: Binance estimates that hackers took about $6.3 billion in a breach disclosed Thursday and Friday, the largest crypto heist on record (Axios, Bloomberg, CNBC). Bloomberg reported that Binance suspended deposits and withdrawals. About $3 billion has been frozen, with Tether, Circle and others also freezing funds (CNBC). Binance says it has set aside more than $6.3 billion of its own funds to cover losses.

Binance's co-CEO said an initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which let an attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance says it has seen no evidence that private keys leaked (CNBC, TechCrunch). That would make the entry point a human and an endpoint, not a break in the exchange's cryptography.

TRM Labs and Elliptic both attribute the theft to North Korean hackers, TechCrunch reports. A TRM investigator said "This was absolutely North Korea," according to the Wall Street Journal as cited in coverage. Elliptic said some funds ended in a wallet used in an earlier attack on the exchange Bitget. Authorities have not confirmed attribution (TechCrunch, Axios).
Markets took it in stride relative to past hacks. Bitcoin slipped below $77,000 and was near $76,820 late Friday (Bloomberg, CNBC, market data).
facts: Binance estimates $6.3 billion was stolen.
About $3 billion has been frozen.
An initial probe points to a compromised engineer's laptop.
Binance says no private keys leaked.
TRM Labs and Elliptic blame North Korean hackers.
stories.next: Watch for official attribution, more recovered funds and whether Binance restores withdrawals.
stories.flag: The $6.3 billion figure is Binance's estimate and may change. North Korean attribution comes from private researchers, not authorities.
stories.why: The largest theft in crypto history started with one engineer's device, which shows that endpoint security and access to production containers can matter more than the cryptography. It also tests how much customers trust exchanges to cover losses.

stories.title: NASA's Swift telescope ends science work and is set to fall back to Earth after a failed rescue
stories.summary: After a private rescue craft failed, Swift stopped observing on Oct. 20 and is expected to re-enter within weeks.
story: NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory made its final observation on Oct. 20 and entered safe mode at about 171 miles (275 km) above Earth, when it could no longer offset the extra drag, NASA says. NASA then sent a command that effectively ended operations to prepare the spacecraft for re-entry, which it expects in the next few weeks. Some researchers predict re-entry on Nov. 2, Nature reports.

A private rescue attempt failed. NASA paid $30 million for the first-of-its-kind mission, Space.com reported. Katalyst Space's LINK craft launched on July 3, but some of its reaction wheels failed soon after, and controllers said on Aug. 19 that LINK would no longer try to capture and boost Swift. NASA says LINK itself re-entered on Sept. 25 (Space.com, NASA).

Increased solar activity heated and expanded the upper atmosphere, raising drag on Swift and speeding its orbital decay. NASA expects most of the spacecraft to burn up, though some components are expected to survive, with debris most likely falling into the ocean. The risk to anyone on Earth is unlikely, NASA says. Nature quotes Swift science operations lead Caryl Gronwall: "There's definitely grief."
Swift observed everything from black holes to gamma-ray bursts, and astronomers are mourning its loss (Nature).
facts: Swift's final observation was Oct. 20.
Swift was at 171 miles (275 km) when it entered safe mode.
LINK launched July 3 and was abandoned for capture on Aug. 19.
Re-entry is expected within weeks, with some researchers predicting Nov. 2.
NASA expects most of Swift to burn up.
stories.next: Watch for NASA's re-entry announcement, possibly as early as Nov. 2.
stories.flag: The Nov. 2 re-entry date is a prediction by some researchers, not a NASA date.
stories.why: Swift's quick-response gamma-ray burst work will be hard to replace, and the failed rescue shows commercial orbit-boosting is not yet proven. Solar activity is now shortening the lives of other low-orbit satellites.

stories.title: Physicists hold a single positron in a trap for months to test matter-antimatter symmetry
stories.summary: Gerald Gabrielse's team cooled one positron to its lowest energy state to measure its magnetic moment with new precision.
story: A Nature news report says Gerald Gabrielse's group at Northwestern trapped a single positron, the electron's antimatter twin, and cooled it to its lowest energy state, keeping it for months. The aim is to measure the positron's magnetic moment with extraordinary precision and compare it with the electron's (Nature). Gabrielse says that finding a mismatch between matter and antimatter would be revolutionary for physics.

The comparison tests a symmetry in physics called CPT. A 2026 arXiv preprint on a one-positron quantum cyclotron says the electron's magnetic moment is the best-measured property of any elementary particle, at about 3 parts in 10 trillion. The positron's is known about 15 times less precisely, so closing that gap is the goal.

Related antimatter measurements are already tight. The antiproton's magnetic moment has been measured to 1.5 parts per billion, and the proton's to 0.3 parts per billion. Nature's Briefing Chat on Oct. 23 covers how the team trapped the particle.
The coverage found does not give the precision the new experiment reached, so the result is a method demonstration for now.
facts: The experiment holds one positron in a trap for months.
The team is led by Gerald Gabrielse at Northwestern.
The goal is to compare positron and electron magnetic moments.
The positron's moment is known about 15 times less precisely than the electron's.
Nature reported the work in late October.
stories.next: Watch for the full measurement and any difference from the electron's value.
stories.flag: The precision reached by the new experiment was not found in the coverage, and the electron-comparison figures come from an arXiv preprint.
stories.why: A matter-antimatter difference would break the Standard Model's symmetry assumptions and could help explain why the universe has more matter. Even a null result tightens one of the most precise tests in physics.

stories.title: Analysts ask what Anthropic's IPO filing leaves out: slower growth, compute costs and a valuation
stories.summary: CNBC lists open questions in the S-1, including about $417 billion in compute obligations and nearly half of revenue flowing through three cloud partners.
story: CNBC reported on Friday that analysts see several gaps in Anthropic's public S-1. The filing does not explain how much it costs to generate each added dollar of revenue as compute demand rises, and growth appears to have slowed in the third quarter, with a Morningstar analyst saying management's outlook on that slowdown was not disclosed (CNBC). About 80% of revenue is consumption-based, which leaves it exposed to swings in usage.

Compute commitments are large. The filing reportedly shows roughly $417 billion in obligations to providers, plus an expected $125 billion to $150 billion more for 2028 to 2031 deals whose pricing is not final. Analysts say it is unclear how much goes to training versus serving customers, and that split will shape margins. Close to half of revenue flows through Microsoft, Amazon and Google cloud channels, and five customers made up about a quarter of revenue in the first nine months of 2026 (CNBC).

Founders hold special voting power through a single share class with 50.1% of votes. The price is not set, and the prospectus says valuation will be "determined by negotiations among us, the selling stockholders, and the representatives." Analyst estimates run from about $1 trillion to more than $2 trillion (CNBC). Bloomberg reports Anthropic is weighing 15% to 20% of shares for retail investors through JPMorgan.
CNBC's earlier coverage cited 900% revenue retention alongside $80 billion in first-half losses, and a mid-October report put third-quarter revenue near $16.8 billion.
facts: The S-1 was filed publicly on Oct. 26 with the ticker ANT.
The filing reportedly shows about $417 billion in compute obligations to providers.
About 80% of revenue is consumption-based.
Five customers made up about a quarter of revenue in the first nine months of 2026.
Founders hold 50.1% of votes through special voting power.
stories.next: Watch for a price range and roadshow, with trading reportedly possible the week of Nov. 16.
stories.flag: Sources disagree on revenue figures (Q2 appears as $10.9 billion in May and $11.56 billion in October) and on the valuation range. Numbers are provisional until checked against the S-1.
stories.why: A listing near $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion would be among the largest ever, and the filing puts AI lab economics, such as compute costs and customer concentration, under public scrutiny. This week's tech selloff makes pricing harder.

stories.title: Nvidia and Reflection push open-weight models as frontier labs pull back on safety grounds
stories.summary: Nvidia released free open models for agents, PCs and transcription, while OpenAI reportedly shelved a model over safety concerns.
story: Nvidia released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe on Wednesday, Oct. 28, a free open-weight model that transcribes recorded audio in up to 40 languages. It handles recordings, not live audio (TechCrunch). On Oct. 19 the company launched open-weight models for enterprise agents and PCs, including the 120-billion-parameter Nemotron 3.5 Super VL. Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, and Bolt E4B was due later in October (TechCrunch).
Nvidia-backed startup Reflection unveiled a powerful open-weight model in early October. Axios expected it to trail the top U.S. models but compete with leading Chinese open models.

Closed labs are under their own pressure. CNBC reported that OpenAI decided not to release GPT-6.1 Astra after finding it did not adequately meet the company's safety standards, and sources name the model inconsistently. On Oct. 8 CNBC reported OpenAI told investors it reached about $50 billion in annualized revenue at the end of September, below an earlier $68 billion figure, and AI stocks including Nvidia fell.
facts: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe supports up to 40 languages and works on recordings.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL has 120 billion parameters.
Bolt 74B-A9B and Super VL are available now.
Reflection is an Nvidia-backed open-weight startup.
OpenAI reportedly shelved GPT-6.1 Astra over safety.
stories.next: Watch for independent benchmarks of Reflection's model and Nvidia's Bolt E4B release.
stories.flag: OpenAI's model name varies across sources (GPT-6 Astra or GPT-6.1 Astra). The OpenAI revenue figure comes from reports of what it told investors.
stories.why: Open-weight models from a chip company and a startup lower the price of agent and speech tools and give developers an alternative to closed APIs. Safety pullbacks at closed labs also raise the question of who decides what gets released.

stories.title: Flu is arriving early as federal vaccine messaging stays thin
stories.summary: Early-October flu positivity ran about six times last year's, and the CDC is promoting shots less than usual.
story: CDC data cited by Axios show flu test positivity at about 3.6% in early October, versus 0.6% at the same point last year. NPR described the season as unusual, starting early and hitting the West rather than the South, and said the early start moves up the best time to get a flu shot (Axios, NPR).

Federal guidance is quieter than usual. On Sept. 2 the CDC extended its 2025 flu vaccine recommendations to this year, and NPR reported the agency has not been promoting flu shots as it normally does. A CDC spokesperson said it is developing a communication strategy. In January the CDC dropped its routine annual flu shot advice for children in favor of shared clinical decision-making, and pediatric groups objected (NPR).

Medical groups have filled the gap. Leading organizations issued their own recommendations for COVID-19, flu and RSV vaccines in September (NPR). A new mRNA flu vaccine is also available this season to adults 50 and older, according to CNN.
facts: Flu positivity was about 3.6% in early October, versus 0.6% a year earlier.
The season is hitting the West earlier than the South, per NPR.
The CDC extended its 2025 flu vaccine recommendations on Sept. 2.
The CDC dropped routine annual flu shots for children in January.
An mRNA flu vaccine is available to adults 50 and older.
stories.next: Watch the CDC's weekly flu updates and whether it launches a vaccination campaign.
stories.flag: The positivity data are from early October, and the coverage found does not include newer CDC numbers.
stories.why: An early season in the West means Bay Area residents may want flu shots sooner than usual. With less federal promotion, local clinics, pharmacies and medical groups carry more of the messaging.

briefs: BART's board picked Pacific Development and Affirmed Housing to build 643 homes, including 176 affordable, on about 12 acres of Fremont station parking lots, with approval hoped for in 2027 and construction in 2028 (SF Chronicle).
Emerson College polling from Oct. 17 to 19 has Xavier Becerra ahead of Republican Steve Hilton 60% to 33% in the California governor's race, and PPIC has a similar gap at 61% to 37% (CalMatters).
IEEE Spectrum reports d-Matrix's Raptor accelerator stacks logic directly on commodity DRAM instead of HBM, cutting data travel from millimeters to micrometers (IEEE Spectrum).
